summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing the Real-Time Transport Protocol, which carries audio and video.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP carries live sound and video. This gives tools a way to check how those streams are doing.

questions: how to monitor rtp with snmp
subtitle: A set of SNMP-readable tables for watching RTP sessions, senders and receivers on hosts and monitors.

tldr.problem: Operators had no standard way to ask an RTP system, through network management tools, which sessions are running and how the streams are doing.
tldr.mechanism: The RTP MIB defines tables of sessions, senders and receivers, plus optional inverse lookup tables, built around the data RTP and RTCP already produce.
tldr.outcome: A network manager can use SNMP to diagnose faults and plan capacity for RTP sessions, and a monitor can even be told to join a session and watch it.

today: RFC 2959 is a Proposed Standard from October 2000 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: What the RTP MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2959 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing systems that use the Real-Time Transport Protocol, defined in RFC 1889. A MIB is a virtual information store that a management protocol such as SNMP can read, and its objects are described with the Structure of Management Information. This module is written in SMIv2.

An "RTP System" is either a host end-system that sends or receives RTP data packets, or an intermediate system that forwards them. RTP monitors may collect RTCP information about the senders and receivers to and from such a host or intermediate system.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a standard list of questions a manager can ask a machine that handles live audio or video, such as who is talking and how well it is going.

sections.title: Sessions, Senders and Receivers
sections.content:
The MIB is built around three ideas taken from RTP. A session is the association of participants communicating with RTP, defined by a pair of destination transport addresses: one network address plus a port pair for RTP and RTCP. A sender is identified within a session by a 32-bit SSRC (synchronization source) value and is the source of a stream of RTP packets and of RTCP Sender Reports. A receiver has an SSRC that is unique to the session and is the source of RTCP Receiver Reports.

For an IP multicast session, all participants share the same address. For a unicast session, each side has a different unicast address.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is a meeting room, a sender is someone talking in it, and a receiver is someone listening and reporting back how well they heard.

sections.title: The Six Tables
sections.content:
There are six tables. The rtpSessionTable describes active sessions at the host or monitor. The rtpSenderTable holds information about senders and the rtpRcvrTable about receivers of session data. Three inverse tables (rtpSessionInverseTable, rtpSenderInverseTable and rtpRcvrInverseTable) help find indexes into those tables.

The inverse tables are optional. Implementors SHOULD implement them for multicast RTP sessions when the table indexes are not available from other MIBs. Otherwise a management application may have to do expensive tree walks through large numbers of sessions, senders or receivers.

The object rtpSessionNewIndex lets a manager obtain a unique index for creating a new row in the session table. The manager reads it, writes the value back in the Set that creates the row, and repeats if the Set fails with inconsistentValue.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three main lists (sessions, senders, receivers) and three optional phone-book style lists that make finding things in the main lists quicker.

sections.title: Hosts and Monitors
sections.content:
The MIB may be used by two kinds of RTP implementation. RTP hosts are end-systems that collect data on streams they send or receive, which a network manager can use to detect and diagnose faults, as in a help-desk scenario. RTP monitors of multicast sessions may be third parties or may sit in a host, and collect statistics for capacity planning and fault diagnosis. Use of the MIB for RTP translators and mixers is left for further study.

The rtpSessionMonitor object says whether remote senders and receivers are to be monitored. When it is true(1), senders and receivers MUST be monitored with entries in the sender and receiver tables, filled from RTCP reports. Monitors MUST initialize it to true(1) and hosts SHOULD initialize it to false(2). A host that also monitors MUST set it to true(1).

A host agent must create a read-only session row for each session it is sending to or receiving from, and delete it when the session is over and no sender or receiver rows remain. A monitor SHOULD allow a manager to create session rows, which has the side effect of making the system join the multicast session to gather data.
sections.plainLanguage: A host is a person in the meeting keeping notes on their own call. A monitor is an observer who listens in on everyone and writes down how the meeting is going.

sections.title: Objects in the Tables
sections.content:
The session table records the transport domain, remote and local addresses, the interface (rtpSessionIfIndex), counts of sender joins, receiver joins and RTCP BYE messages, the start time and the monitor flag. Five session objects are read-create, and a row created by a manager is removed by setting rtpSessionRowStatus to destroy(6).

The sender table, indexed by session and SSRC, holds the CNAME, source address, packet and octet counts (64-bit), the tool name, a count and time of RTCP Sender Reports, and the payload type of the most recent packet. The receiver table, indexed by session, source SSRC and receiver SSRC, holds the CNAME, address, round trip time, lost packets, jitter, tool, a count and time of RTCP Receiver Reports, payload type, and packet and octet counts.

The round trip time can give meaningful results only when the agent has the same clock as the stream sender. Otherwise the entity should answer noSuchInstance.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row is like a report card: for every speaker it counts packets sent, and for every listener it counts packets lost and how bumpy the delivery was.

sections.title: Groups and Compliance
sections.content:
The objects are divided into groups. The system group holds objects available to all RTP systems. The host group holds objects that hosts have but monitors may not, such as the local address, payload types, round trip time and received packet and octet counts. The monitor group holds rtpSessionNewIndex and rtpSessionRowStatus, used to create session rows; they are not needed if the system does not create rows. The inverse group covers the optional tables.

Host implementations MUST comply with the system and host groups, and may support row creation so that a host can act as a monitor. Monitor implementations must comply with the system and monitor groups, and are not required to support creation or deletion. A monitor that sees only RTCP may not be able to supply payload type or RTP octet and packet counts.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts and monitors each get a checklist of things they must show and things they may skip, because a watcher cannot always see everything a player can.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that a MIB is itself a tool, not a threat, if SNMP security works as intended. Still, read-write and read-create objects can be sensitive, and write access to rtpSessionNewIndex and the five read-create session objects affects how a monitor operates and should be under an access control policy. Read-only objects such as the CNAME may be sensitive in some enterprises, since they can reveal configuration and services.

Encrypting RTCP packets can be a problem for third-party monitors. The RFC points out that RTP allows a compound RTCP packet to be split so that, for example, SDES information is encrypted while reception reports are sent in the clear. SNMPv1 alone is not secure, and implementers are recommended to consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575).
sections.plainLanguage: The dashboard could show private details or let someone change settings, so only the right people should be allowed to look or touch.

viz.caption: THE SIX TABLES OF THE RTP MIB

items.title: rtpSessionTable
items.text: Active sessions at the host or monitor.

items.title: rtpSenderTable
items.text: Senders to an RTP session, indexed by session and SSRC.

items.title: rtpRcvrTable
items.text: Receivers of session data, per sender and receiver SSRC.

items.title: Session inverse table
items.text: Optional lookup into the session table by address.

items.title: Sender inverse table
items.text: Optional lookup into the sender table by sender address.

items.title: Receiver inverse table
items.text: Optional lookup into the receiver table by receiver address.
